t.1.11.1: Formerly I had a friend, a brahmin named Khagama, my dear son, who was exceedingly sharp of speech and endowed with the power of austerity.
t.1.11.2: In my boyhood, while playing, I made a snake out of grass, and with it I frightened him as he was absorbed in the agnihotra; terrified, he fell into a swoon.
t.1.11.3: And having regained consciousness, that ascetic rich in austerities, truthful in speech and firm in his vows, spoke to me as though burning me up with his anger.
t.1.11.4: Of just such strength as this snake that you made to frighten me, of that same strength a serpent you shall become through my anger.
t.1.11.5: Knowing the might of his asceticism, O you whose wealth is austerity, I, my heart greatly agitated, spoke to that forest-dweller.
t.1.11.7: "You ought to forgive me, O brahmin; let this curse be turned back." Then he, seeing me greatly agitated in mind, said to me:
t.1.11.6: Composed yet flustered, standing bowed with joined palms, I said: “Laughing, I did this to you as your friend, only for the sake of a jest.”
t.1.11.8: Sighing hot breaths again and again, the ascetic rich in austerity, greatly agitated, said: "What I have spoken is no falsehood; this shall come to pass in some way."
t.1.11.9: But hear from me the words that I shall speak to you, O you who are firm in your vows; and having heard them, let these words abide in your heart, O you whose wealth is austerity.
t.1.11.10: There will be born a pure son of Pramati, Ruru by name; upon seeing him, your release from the curse will come about before long.
t.1.11.11: You are that pure son of Pramati, known as Ruru. Having regained my own form, today I shall tell you what is for your good.
t.1.11.12: Non-violence is remembered as the highest dharma of all living beings. Therefore a brāhmaṇa should never harm any living creature anywhere.
t.1.11.13: A brāhmaṇa is born here gentle indeed; such is the supreme revelation, dear son: knowing the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, he grants freedom from fear to all beings.
t.1.11.14: Non-violence, truthful speech, and forbearance: this is firmly established as the highest dharma of a brāhmaṇa, higher even than the preserving of the Vedas.
t.1.11.16: Listen to me, Ruru, you whose self is righteous: this killing of the snakes in former times was indeed the deed of a kṣatriya, of Janamejaya.
t.1.11.15: But the dharma that belongs to a kṣatriya is truly not sought for you here: wielding the rod of punishment, fierceness, and the protection of the people.
t.1.11.17: And the rescue of the frightened snakes at the snake sacrifice came from a brahmin, O best of the twice-born: from Āstīka, foremost of the twice-born, endowed with the might and strength of austerity and gone to the far shore of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
